"The wagon starts across at two, when the road opens, with Kit and me beside it in plain sight, and Corvin visible on the bench. Your six stay in the reeds until I raise my lantern-staff, and then they close both ends of the culvert."

I tuck the bait tube into my cloak where it will show when I move, and I keep Faerie Fire ready for the first man who steps out of the shed.

input.add_to_description: Day 15 ~1 PM: Marl crossed the flats unseen (Stealth 19) and reached the longboat, but her check to pull the bung and haul the oars was only 10 (DC 12): she got the oars off one side but the bung stuck and the boat still floats. She slipped back before anyone noticed. Wren will start the wagon across at about 2 PM, bait tube visible in her cloak, with Pell's six lying in the landward reeds until she raises the lamp-staff.

entries.text: notebook: updated Gannet Causeway

Marl nods once and is gone into the reeds. She is back in the best part of an hour, mud to the thighs, and she reports it in her flat voice. Nobody saw her go. At the longboat she got the oars off one side and dragged them up the bank, but the bung was swollen tight and would not come, and she dared not hammer at it. Her check was a 10, short of the 12 it needed. The longboat still floats, with only half its oars. If the master runs, he can still row, slowly and lopsided.

You tell Pell the order: the wagon crosses when the road opens, and his six stay in the reeds until you raise the lamp-staff. Then they close both ends of the culvert. Pell grunts and sends them down. You tuck the bait tube into your cloak where the sealed wax shows when you move.

Around two, the water pulls back off the timber edging and the causeway shines wet and open. The wagon creaks onto it with Corvin visible on the bench, shackled feet and open hands, and gulls scatter ahead of the horses. You walk Ember on one side, Kit on the other, lamp-staff upright in your hand. The far bank and its drowned shed come closer, grey and silent. It is nearly two in the afternoon, and you are a third of the way out.

You've three slots, three Inspirations, and Faerie Fire ready. Nothing has stirred at the shed. Ahead is the culvert, where the road narrows to one cart-width. What does Wren do?

sheet.name: Wren Ashgrove
sheet.opening: Wren Ashgrove, a half-elf bard of about nineteen with a quick grin and a sharper tongue, arrives at dusk in the river-market town of Marrowford, a few weeks after fleeing the caravan of her mentor Corvin Tallowmere. She was raised by him as a storyteller's apprentice, and she left in the night at a river crossing with his ledger of forged tales sold to nobles (its pages now hidden in the binding of her road-psalter), a few of his best forgeries, and a head start. She carries a brass lantern-shaped reliquary of the Lantern-Bearer, a gentle road-god of travelers and tale-tellers whom Corvin worshipped only as cover; it holds a curl of yellowed parchment in an unknown hand that may be a true blessing or another forgery. She does not know if Corvin has sent anyone after her. Her ideal: stories should be free, and truth is whatever people can be made to believe. Her bond: find the nobles Corvin cheated and decide whether to expose him or quietly fix what he did. Her flaw: she can't resist a secret, and she lies even when the truth would serve her better. She has 15 gp, a rapier, a dagger, leather armor, a lute, a diplomat's pack with blank paper and sealing wax, and was raised with no memory of her birth family. The hook: as she reaches the market square, she spots a caravan wagon with Corvin's painted shrine-lantern sigil parked at the edge of town, but no sign of Corvin. A frightened young page in a minor noble's livery is pressing a sealed letter into the hands of the wagon's driver, and the seal looks like one Wren has seen in the ledger. Something is happening that links her stolen ledger to a noble house, and it needs a quick-witted liar to either sort it out or be caught in it. Open on Wren in the square, with the choice of how to approach the wagon and the page, and a locked iron-bound strongbox on the wagon's tailboard that she itches to poke at.

Bardic Inspiration (d6): You can inspire others through stirring words or music. To do so, you use a bonus action on your turn to choose one creature other than yourself within 60 feet of you who can hear you. That creature gains one Bardic Inspiration die, a d6. Once within the next 10 minutes, the creature can roll the die and add the number rolled to one ability check, attack roll, or saving throw it makes. The creature can wait until after it rolls the d20 before deciding to use the Bardic Inspiration die, but must decide before the GM says whether the roll succeeds or fails. Once the Bardic Inspiration die is rolled, it is lost. A creature can have only one Bardic Inspiration die at a time. Your Bardic Inspiration die changes when you reach certain levels in this class. The die becomes a d8 at 5th level, a d10 at 10th level, and a d12 at 15th level. Song of Rest (d6): Beginning at 2nd level, you can use soothing music or oration to help revitalize your wounded allies during a short rest. If you or any friendly creatures who can hear your performance regain hit points at the end of the short rest by spending one or more Hit Dice, each of those creatures regains an extra 1d6 hit points.  The extra hit points increase when you reach certain levels in this class: to 1d8 at 9th level, to 1d10 at 13th level, and to 1d12 at 17th level. At level 2: extra 1d6 hit points.

You and your adventuring companions can expect to receive free healing and care at a temple, shrine, or other established presence of your faith, though you must provide any material components needed for spells. Those who share your religion will support you (but only you) at a modest lifestyle. You might also have ties to a specific temple dedicated to your chosen deity or pantheon, and you have a residence there. This could be the temple where you used to serve, if you remain on good terms with it, or a temple where you have found a new home. While near your temple, you can call upon the priests for assistance, provided the assistance you ask for is not hazardous and you remain in good standing with your temple.

entries.text: dice Marl Sedge's Stealth reaching the longboat across the far-bank creek, vs the lookout's passive Perception 13: 1d20+6 = 1d20 [7] + 6 = 13

Marl gives her flat nod and is gone into the reeds. Your Persuasion isn't needed. She works her way up the channel to where it narrows and wades it, and the far-bank lookout's passive Perception is 13. Her Stealth check is exactly 13, which is just enough. She is across, unseen by a hair.

Over the next hour you wait with the wagon at the causeway mouth while the water draws back off the gravel. You set the plan with Pell. The wagon starts across at two with you and Kit beside it, and Corvin sits visible on the bench. His feet are shackled, his hands are free, and he is humming the road song. The six guards stay in the landward reeds until you raise the lamp-staff, and then they close both ends of the culvert. You tuck the bait tube into your cloak so it shows when you move.

A little before two, Marl slides back out of the reeds, wet to the thighs. She says the two oars are in the mud of the bank. She pulled the bung from the longboat, and it is settling at its mooring with a hand's depth of water in her. "They won't row that anywhere soon," she says, and then adds, "I think the lookout saw a ripple. He looked a long time at the creek, then went in."

The causeway is bare now, a wet gravel line nine hundred paces long under a hard white sky. At the far end the boat-shed door stands shut. The tide has just turned, and the bank is clear. It is two o'clock. You have three slots, all your Inspirations, Faerie Fire ready, and the lamp-staff in your hand. Kit stands at the lead horse's head. Corvin looks at you from the bench and lifts one eyebrow.

What does Wren do?

input.add_to_description: Day 15 ~12:30 PM: wounded in the thigh by a crossbow bolt while trying to disable the longboat; bound up and resting in the reeds. Not fit to fight.

entries.text: notebook: updated Marl Sedge

Marl gives her flat nod and goes. She is good, but the die isn't kind: her Stealth check is a 9 against a lookout's passive 13. A shout goes up from the creek mouth, a crossbow cracks, and a little later she crawls back into the landward reeds with a bolt through her thigh and her teeth set. Pell's guards bind it. She will live, but she can't fight, and she mutters, "They know the bank's watched."

So the longboat is untouched, and the shed is awake. You decide the plan still stands, since the master wants the tube and has more men than he needs for show. Pell lays out the last details in a low voice. His six stay in the reeds until you raise the lamp-staff, and then they close both ends of the culvert. You tuck the bait tube into your cloak where its wax shows when you move. You keep Faerie Fire ready, with three slots and three Inspirations in hand.

The water drains slowly off the gravel, and the timber edging dries from black to grey. A little before two the first dry stretch shows at the landward end, and by two the whole causeway lies bare, a long pale line across the silver flats. On the far bank, in the doorway of the drowned boat-shed, a lean figure in a brown coat steps into the light and stands there, hands empty, plainly visible. He tips his hat.

Corvin sits upright on the wagon bench, hands in his lap and his shackled feet on the boards. He doesn't look at the shed. "Now," he says quietly, "they will wait for the middle. He always does."

It is two in the afternoon on Day 15. The wagon, Kit, Pell, and you stand at the causeway mouth, with six guards hidden in the reeds. What does Wren do?

A frightened young page in a minor noble's livery is pressing a sealed letter into the hands of the wagon's driver, and the seal looks like one Wren has seen in the ledger. Something is happening that links her stolen ledger to a noble house, and it needs a quick-witted liar to either sort it out or be caught in it. Open on Wren in the square, with the choice of how to approach the wagon and the page, and a locked iron-bound strongbox on the wagon's tailboard that she itches to poke at.

features: Darkvision: You have superior vision in dark and dim conditions. You can see in dim light within 60 feet of you as if it were bright light, and in darkness as if it were dim light. You cannot discern color in darkness, only shades of gray.
Fey Ancestry: You have advantage on saving throws against being charmed, and magic cannot put you to sleep.
Skill Versatility: You gain proficiency in two skills of your choice.

Bardic Inspiration (d6): You can inspire others through stirring words or music. To do so, you use a bonus action on your turn to choose one creature other than yourself within 60 feet of you who can hear you. That creature gains one Bardic Inspiration die, a d6. Once within the next 10 minutes, the creature can roll the die and add the number rolled to one ability check, attack roll, or saving throw it makes. The creature can wait until after it rolls the d20 before deciding to use the Bardic Inspiration die, but must decide before the GM says whether the roll succeeds or fails. Once the Bardic Inspiration die is rolled, it is lost. A creature can have only one Bardic Inspiration die at a time. You can use this feature a number of times equal to your Charisma modifier (a minimum of once). You regain any expended uses when you finish a long rest.  Your Bardic Inspiration die changes when you reach certain levels in this class. The die becomes a d8 at 5th level, a d10 at 10th level, and a d12 at 15th level. At level 2: Bardic Inspiration die d6.
Jack of All Trades: Starting at 2nd level, you can add half your proficiency bonus, rounded down, to any ability check you make that doesn't already include your proficiency bonus.

Song of Rest (d6): Beginning at 2nd level, you can use soothing music or oration to help revitalize your wounded allies during a short rest. If you or any friendly creatures who can hear your performance regain hit points at the end of the short rest by spending one or more Hit Dice, each of those creatures regains an extra 1d6 hit points.  The extra hit points increase when you reach certain levels in this class: to 1d8 at 9th level, to 1d10 at 13th level, and to 1d12 at 17th level. At level 2: extra 1d6 hit points.

Shelter of the Faithful (Acolyte): As an acolyte, you command the respect of those who share your faith, and you can perform the religious ceremonies of your deity. You and your adventuring companions can expect to receive free healing and care at a temple, shrine, or other established presence of your faith, though you must provide any material components needed for spells. Those who share your religion will support you (but only you) at a modest lifestyle. You might also have ties to a specific temple dedicated to your chosen deity or pantheon, and you have a residence there. This could be the temple where you used to serve, if you remain on good terms with it, or a temple where you have found a new home. While near your temple, you can call upon the priests for assistance, provided the assistance you ask for is not hazardous and you remain in good standing with your temple.

spellcasting.notes: Spells known are fixed until a level-up.
